home.heroSubtitle: How Oman Reconnects With Its Wadis
home.section1Heading: When Cities Block Natural Water Flow
home.section1Body1: Oman has witnessed several floods in recent decades, some of which had a widespread impact on the population and infrastructure.
home.section1Body2: The risks are concentrated in urban areas that have expanded near wadi streams.
home.keyResultsIntro: This reduces water infiltration and leads to:
home.keyResultsNote: In areas near wadis, this significantly increases flood risk and reduces natural protection.
characteristicsList: Large volumes of water in a short time
Often carry debris, rocks, and sediment
home.characteristicsNote: These features make wadis particularly dangerous when urban development expands close to their natural paths.
home.impactsBody: Floods cause damage to homes and infrastructure, disrupt livelihoods, and lead to costly recovery efforts for both communities and government.
home.planningBody: What is needed in urban planning is to protect natural water flow paths when designing urban areas. Sustainable drainage systems and permeable surfaces should be included to reduce flooding risks. It is also important to avoid building in flood-prone zones.
rainfallList: During Cyclone Shaheen 2021, rainfall in parts of Bawshar was estimated between 120–250 mm within 24–48 hours.
Short-duration storm intensity reached approximately 40–60 mm/hour during peak rainfall periods.
Flash flood response time in wadis within Bawshar (e.g., Al Ansab) is typically 30–60 minutes after intense rainfall.
Wadi water levels during peak flow events reached approximately 1–2.5 meters depending on channel capacity.
Floodwater spread in low-lying urban areas extended roughly 30–150 meters from wadi channels.
riskCitiesList: Areas like Al-Ansab are considered highly sensitive due to the proximity of urban development to wadi beds.
Localized flooding affected residential neighborhoods and road networks in Bawshar.
Temporary road closures occurred in underpasses and near wadi crossings.
Property-level impacts ranged from minor water intrusion to significant structural damage in some cases.

recommended.title: Stop Flooding by Thinking Like a Sponge
recommended.intro: The Main Idea: Don't try to get rid of rainwater quickly. Instead, let the city act like a sponge — absorb the water, store it temporarily, then release it slowly.

items.title: Small Home Cisterns (Aljibes)
items.body: Encourage every house to have a small, underground tank to collect rainwater from the roof. If 1,000 homes store 20 cubic meters each, that's 20,000 cubic meters of floodwater removed from the streets.

items.title: Tree Pits as Mini-Reservoirs
items.body: Plant trees in large pits filled with gravel, not just soil. These pits act as underground tanks, storing water and feeding the tree.

items.title: Permeable Pavement
items.body: Replace solid asphalt with porous blocks in parking lots and quiet streets. Water goes through the pavement into the ground below.

items.title: Open, Shallow Canals (Acequias)
items.body: Instead of hiding water in pipes, use beautiful, open, shallow canals to guide water. These slow down the flow and allow water to soak into the sides.

items.title: Rain Gardens (Sickermulden)
items.body: Create shallow, plant-filled depressions in low points of parks or public areas. These gardens are designed to flood temporarily during a storm.

items.title: Empty Before the Storm
items.body: Connect storage tanks to a simple sensor and weather forecast. If a big storm is coming, the system automatically empties the tanks before the rain starts, so they are empty and ready to capture the floodwater.

items.title: Floodable Parks (Wadis)
items.body: Design parks in low-lying areas as "floodable zones." During normal weather, they are soccer fields or gardens. During heavy rain, they safely fill with water like a bathtub, protecting the surrounding houses.

recommended.caseStudyHeading: Sustainable Drainage Concept from Sultan Haitham City
recommended.caseStudyBody: A low-impact development approach manages rainwater by mimicking the natural water cycle, allowing runoff to slow down, spread, and infiltrate through green and permeable surfaces rather than being rapidly discharged. It focuses on low-slope areas, where floodwater tends to accumulate, and uses gravity-based drainage supported by natural landform design. Designed using hydrological modeling and historical extreme events, the system can handle rainfall of up to 250 mm per day. This approach represents a resilient model that could be gradually applied in existing cities to reduce flood risks near wadis.

damageCost.title: Damages Cost
damageCost.savingsHeading: Estimated Flood Damage Savings Using Cyclone Shaheen Data
damageCost.savingsBody: Cyclone Shaheen caused about 300 million OMR in damage, mostly near major wadis. Assuming 50% of losses occur close to wadis, the 26,602 buildings within 1 km of Wadi Al-Ansab face roughly 150 million OMR in potential damage per major flood. Restricting construction in this zone could have avoided most of these losses in Bawshar. Over multiple flood events, total avoided damage could reach up to 450 million OMR.
damageCost.exposureBody: Based on the weighted overlay results, areas within 1 km of the main wadi streams were classified as high flood-exposure zones. All buildings located within these zones were extracted and counted. The analysis shows that by the end of 2018, 26,602 buildings were constructed within this high-exposure area in Bawshar Wilayat.

about.title: Wadi Wise
about.tagline: Our goal is to enable smarter site selection in Oman by avoiding wadi flood risks using GIS.
about.visionBody: Our goal is to enable smarter site selection in Oman by leveraging GIS technology to identify and avoid wadi-related flood risks, ensuring safer and more resilient development investments.
about.missionBody: Our mission is to use accurate spatial data to identify wadi flood risks, guide safer site selection, and support informed decisions, while also assessing existing developments and reducing risks to enhance community safety using GIS.
